## Overview

In this graded assignment, you will practice with shell scripts,
running software with containers, rendering Markdown with Pandoc,
and version control with Git and GitHub.

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Oct 11^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: You will submit your assignment by tagging the instructors in an
  Issue in your GitHub repository, as per the last step below.

::: callout-note
#### Oral examination
For one of the three remaining graded assignments (this one, GA3, and GA4–GA5),
each of you will be asked to explain your work in a short oral examination.
You won't know in advance which assignment this will be.
We'll ask you to walk us through how you approached a few of the questions
and to explain your answers.

If you can explain and justify what you submitted, this should be straightforward.
If it's clear that you don't understand your own answer to a question,
you'll receive no points for that question.
If this is the case for several questions,
you may be asked to redo the assignment.

We'll use 15-minute time slots for the oral examinations,
and we'll schedule them after the assignment deadline.
We'd also like to use a few minutes of this time to hear about your overall
experience with the course so far (this part is not graded).
:::

### Rubric

You can earn a maximum of **0.5 points** for each of the 20 numbered questions/items below.

There are two **bonus** questions (21 and 22) that can also earn you 0.5 points
each, but only in case you dropped points elsewhere.

## Detailed steps

### General

- We provide a **template** `README.md`
  (see "Setting up" below) with a section for each question,
  where you can add your answers:
  - Add the commands you ran only where the template has a `bash` code block for them.
  - Include a command's output only where the template has an output block for it.

- For each **shell script** you write, follow the practices from class:
  start with the shebang and safe-settings lines,
  and copy any placeholder variables like `$1` to descriptively named variables.
  You don't need to paste your scripts into your README,
  since we'll look at them in your repo.

- In any question where you're asked to make **predictions**, and then to run commands
  to check your predictions, no points will be subtracted for any incorrect predictions.

- _Recommended_: Keep a Markdown preview open to the side,
  so you can check that it renders as you intended.

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code (Code Server) session at OSC OnDemand as per usual,
  and open a terminal in that session.

- Create a new dir for this assignment, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA3`,
  and navigate there.
  *This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.*

- Copy the **template file** for this assignment,
  `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA3/GA3_template.md`,
  into your working dir as `README.md`
  (keep this exact file name --- so don't include, e.g., your own name).
  _You'll use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers._

### Part A: Your README, data, and Git repo

01. Inside dir `GA3`, create subdirs `data`, `scripts`, and `results`.
    Then, copy some files into your GA3 "project"^[So your dir is self-contained,
    as would be typical when working on a research project.]:

    ```bash
    # Copy your FastQC results into your `results` dir:
    cp -r ../week07/results/fastqc results/

    # Copy the Garrigós metadata file into your `data` dir:
    cp ../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv data/
    ```

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Help! I don't have those FastQC results.</summary>
    You may not have those FastQC results
    (perhaps we didn't get that far in class, or you didn't manage to follow along).
    In that case, you can copy files from the share dir instead, as follows:

    ```bash
    # Copy some FastQC results into your `results` dir:
    cp -r /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA3/results/fastqc results/
    ```

    </details>

    _Optional:_ Take a look at the structure of your GA3 dir after copying those files,
    for example using the `tree` command.
    Your `results/fastqc` dir should contain several dozen files.

02. Initialize a **Git repository**,
    and in a first commit, commit your `README.md` file (and nothing else).
    Then, create a `.gitignore` file that makes Git ignore the `data` and `results`
    dirs, and commit this file.

03. **_Throughout the assignment_**, commit your files to your Git repo as you go along,
    using informative commit messages.
    Besides the specific commits that questions ask for,
    commit at least once per Part.

### Part B: Basic shell scripts

04. Save the code below in a script `scripts/echo.sh`.
    Then, look at the four commands below that will run the script,
    and for each, describe what you expect to be the output and why.

    - The script:

      ```{.bash .file filename="scripts/echo.sh"}
      #!/bin/bash
      set -euo pipefail

      echo "$1"
      echo "$2"
      echo "$3"
      echo "Finished"


      ```

    - The commands to run the script four times with different arguments:

      ```bash
      bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08
      bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 Oct09 Oct10
      bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 "Oct09 Oct10"
      bash scripts/echo.sh results/fastqc/*.html
      ```

05. Run the commands, and if any output differed from your prediction,
    try to understand and explain why.

06. Write a shell script `scripts/printline.sh` that accepts two arguments,
    \(1) an input file path and (2) a line number.
    The script should **print** (not store in a file) the requested line from the
    specified file and nothing else.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for a hint.</summary>
    Figure out a way to combine `head` and `tail` with a pipe to print one
    specific line from a file. If you don't manage to,
    your script can instead print all lines up until the specified line,
    so you can still move on to the next question.
    </details>

07. Test your `printline.sh` script **twice**.
    Each time, make it print one line from the `data/metadata.tsv` file you copied earlier.
    In **one** of these tests, _redirect_ the script's output to an appropriately
    named file in the `results` dir, and then check the contents of that file.

### Part C: A script to run MultiQC

MultiQC is a very useful program that summarizes per-sample results of FastQC
and other bioinformatics programs into a single multi-sample report.
This allows you to easily compare results across multiple samples.

MultiQC takes a path to a **directory** as input,
and it will recursively search that directory for files that it can summarize,
such as FastQC results. It will then write its summary report to an output directory.

08. MultiQC isn't available as an OSC module (_optional_: verify this).
    Get a link from the Seqera Containers website to a **container** with the most
    recent version of MultiQC (`bioconda::multiqc` is the correct hit).

09. Print MultiQC's help info by running `multiqc --help` with your container link.
    Use the help info to figure out how to run MultiQC with `results/fastqc` as its
    input dir and `results/multiqc` as its output dir,
    and write down that command in your `README.md` (don't run it yet).

10. Write a script, `scripts/multiqc.sh`, to run MultiQC using the command you
    wrote above.
    That is, the script will have the input and output paths "hard-coded" in it.
    _Optional_: add some logging statements to the script with `echo`,
    like we did in class for the `fastqc.sh` script.

11. Run your script to summarize the FastQC results with MultiQC.
    MultiQC will print logging information to the screen ---
    how many FastQC reports does it say it found,
    and does that match what you expected?
    Commit your `scripts/multiqc.sh` script now that you know it works.

12. Change your `scripts/multiqc.sh` script so that it accepts
    **two arguments**, the input dir and the output dir,
    and uses these when running MultiQC.
    Then, rerun your script, passing the same input and output dirs as before
    (`results/fastqc` and `results/multiqc`) as arguments.
    Commit your updated script to Git,
    so your Git history will now contain both versions of the script.

13. Compare the second MultiQC run with the first one:
    do you notice any differences in what MultiQC printed to the screen,
    and in the names of the output files it created? What caused these differences?

### Part D: Pandoc to render Markdown

So far, you've seen Markdown rendered in VS Code's preview and on GitHub.
But you haven't yet converted ("rendered") any of your Markdown files
to another format, like HTML or PDF, yourself.
The command-line program **Pandoc** can do this for you.
That's handy when, for example, you want to share your notes with someone who
doesn't use Markdown.

14. Here is a Pandoc command to render a Markdown file to PDF:

    ```bash
    pandoc -o README.pdf README.md
    ```

    Take a close look at the **structure of this command**:
    how would you describe it in terms of the option(s) and argument(s) it takes,
    and what does each do?
    Also, how do you think Pandoc knows which output format to produce?

15. Run the above command to **render** your `README.md` to PDF,
    and check that the PDF file was created.
    Then, based on your answer to the previous question,
    write and run a command to render your `README.md` to **HTML** instead.

16. Think about whether the rendered files you just produced should be committed
    to your Git repo or not, and explain your choice.

17. To view PDF files in VS Code,
    you'll need to install the **extension** "_PDF Viewer_" by "Mathematic Inc".
    Install it. Then, simply clicking on the PDF file in the VS Code
    file explorer will open it properly in a new editor tab.
    Make one observation about the rendered PDF file,
    like any formatting you hadn't expected.
    _Optional_: If you see any formatting errors, update your Markdown file,
    rerender the PDF, and check again.

    ![](/img/vscode-pdf-extension.png){fig-align="center" width="50%" fig-alt="PDF Viewer extension for VS Code" .lightbox}

### Part E: Publish your repo on GitHub

Finally, you'll publish your Git repo on GitHub and "hand in" your assignment
by creating an Issue.

18. Create a new, empty, public repository on **GitHub**.
    The repo's name is up to you, but I'd suggest "GA3" or "PLNTPTH5006-GA3"^[
      As pointed out in class, the GitHub repo's name does not need to match the
      name of your local dir.
      As a matter of fact, Git doesn't care about the name of your local dir,
      and your local repo doesn't really have a name at all --- just a location.
    ].

19. Make sure you have committed your final `README.md`.
    Then, connect the GitHub repo to your local repo,
    and push your local repo to GitHub.

    _Your `README.md` will appear in a nicely rendered form on your repo's GitHub page,_
    _so this is another opportunity to review your document_
    _(and if needed, make final adjustments by editing the file in VS Code,_
    _committing the changes, and pushing to GitHub again)._

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for help if you don't want to make the GitHub repo public.</summary>

    - First, I'd reconsider,
      since you're allowed to delete the repo as soon as your grade is in ---
      and more broadly, there is little reason to make your repo private,
      since it contains no sensitive information.

    - If you still want to make it private, you can do so, but then you'll need to
      add the instructors as collaborators to your repo, so we can see it and grade it.

    - To do this, go to your repo's GitHub page,
      click on "Settings" > "Collaborators" > "Add people",
      and add GitHub users `kstarr791` and `jelmerp`.
      Also create an Issue in your repo, as instructed below.

    </details>

20. On the GitHub page for your repo, create a new **Issue**.
    Use whatever title you like, and in the text box (not the title),
    tag GitHub users `kstarr791` and `jelmerp`,
    asking Kelsey and Jelmer to take a look at your assignment.

### Bonus

21. Because it has lots of interactive elements,
    the MultiQC report doesn't render very well in the VS Code preview.
    Therefore, it's better to **download the file** and open it in a web browser
    on your own computer.
    Find one of the MultiQC reports in the VS Code file explorer, right-click on it,
    and you should see a "**_Download..._**" item.
    Click on it to download the file, and open it^[
      After it downloads, your browser will likely show a pop-up where you can
      click on the file name to open it in a web browser.
      Otherwise, use your computer's file browser to navigate to the downloaded file,
      and double-click on it to open it in your browser.
      You're likely familiar with this process.
    ].

    Then, explore the MultiQC report, and try to make sense of it.
    Note that there is lots of interactivity,
    and you can for example see sample IDs when you hover over lines and bars.
    Name one insight you gained from it,
    and one thing you're confused about and would like to learn more about.

22. Check the version of Pandoc that is available at OSC without loading any modules,
    i.e. the one you used above, by running `pandoc -v`.
    Then, search the internet to check if that Pandoc version is the most recent one.
    Check what other versions of Pandoc are available via OSC modules,
    and load the module with the most recent available Pandoc version.
    Finally, run `pandoc -v` again to confirm that you're now using a different version.
